thread.title: Project Thread 1: Optimization and hyperparameter transfer
thread.content: <document version="2.0"><paragraph>This thread exists to help students form teams in this thread as well as deconflict what exactly you want to do. The main document introducing projects has some examples of what can be proposed. <bold>This particular project thread is particularly amenable for having the projects have a bit of life after the semester ends to pull things together into a paper that expounds on this story with a set of systematic explorations.</bold> Consequently, there is a lot of value to be had by deconflicting early and making sure that you get fuller coverage. Everyone whose project contributes to the paper will be a co-author. In previous semesters, I have taught a follow-on special topics course the subsequent semester to help students further develop their projects if they want to. I hope to do that again in the Spring but obviously, that is not required in any way to pursue this option. It's perfectly fine to have a project that ends once the course is done. </paragraph></document>

Hello! I'm Nico (he/him), a senior in CS and Math.

Professionally, I've TA'd for Data 140 and currently do research with the Space Sciences Lab, where I work on the computing systems and analysis pipelines for a new telescope array that studies ultra-high-energy gamma rays. My coursework and projects have covered a lot of the stack, from FPGAs and modern computer architecture to operating systems and distributed systems.

My friends Benji, Jason, and I are a team of three looking for a fourth person. We all have strong math and CS backgrounds and are interested in doing an optimizer-focused project.

While we're still brainstorming and would be open to suggestions and other ideas, some of the questions we're considering include:

Are newer optimizers like Lion or Muon really a straightforward improvement over AdamW, or are their benefits more nuanced? For this, we'd run experiments to explore how sensitive metrics like validation loss are to changes in hyperparameters for variants of the newer optimizers and AdamW.

Can Muon outperform AdamW on Mamba? A lot of the Muon work seems focused on transformers, so an open question appears to be how much better Muon-like optimizers can train Mamba models compared to the default of AdamW (if at all). So we're thinking about 1) getting Mamba to train with Muon, and (time permitting) 2) exploring how the optimum Muon learning rate changes as a function of model depth.

Edit:

Thank you to everyone who reached out! We'll send a connection email soon to help you form groups, since your schedules and interests are likely to align.

We've completed our group and are no longer looking for a fourth member. 

We're looking for a fourth teammate who is curious, collaborative, and excited to experiment with us.

Logistics:

We regularly attend the Wednesday 4-5 PM discussion and plan to meet at least once a week to sync up. Above is a screenshot of our general availability, so if your schedule aligns well with ours, we'd love to hear from you.

If you're interested in working together, please send us a group email! nraultwang@berkeley.edu, bvanlienden@berkeley.edu, jasontrinh@berkeley.edu

comments.content: <document version="2.0"><paragraph>Hi everyone!</paragraph><paragraph>We want to deconflict our idea for a final project in optimizers/hyperparameters. Our group: Sammie Smith, Beth Polito, Kithmini Herath, and I are thinking of working on Critical Batch Size (<link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.06162"><underline>https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.06162</underline></link>, <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.23971"><underline>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.23971</underline></link>) for some of the new optimizers that have emerged. Critical Batch Size has been well studied for AdamW and recently Muon (<link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01598"><underline>https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01598</underline></link>), but many of these newer optimizers still lack some investigation on that front. We are thinking about studying CBS for optimizers like SOAP, Lion, and Sham Kakade’s new optimizer (full Gauss-Newton <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.09378"><underline>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.09378</underline></link>), while also reproducing AdamW and Muon results. Please let us know if you have any ideas or feedback!</paragraph></document>

Hi everyone!

We want to deconflict our idea for a final project in optimizers/hyperparameters. Our group: Sammie Smith, Beth Polito, Kithmini Herath, and I are thinking of working on Critical Batch Size (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.06162, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.23971) for some of the new optimizers that have emerged. Critical Batch Size has been well studied for AdamW and recently Muon (https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01598), but many of these newer optimizers still lack some investigation on that front. We are thinking about studying CBS for optimizers like SOAP, Lion, and Sham Kakade’s new optimizer (full Gauss-Newton https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.09378), while also reproducing AdamW and Muon results. Please let us know if you have any ideas or feedback!

comments.content: <document version="2.0"><paragraph>Hi guys! </paragraph><paragraph>Our group—Micah Mok, Rahul Bir, Ethan Stone, and Devan Perkash—will be exploring the latest manifold muon optimizer (<link href="https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/modular-manifolds/"><underline>https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/modular-manifolds/</underline></link>). In a similar style to the “Muon is scalable for LLM training” Kimi paper (<link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.16982"><underline>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.16982</underline></link>), we will be training an LLM from scratch and seeing if we can get manifold muon to converge. To deconflict, we'll outline our tentative project plan.
We are focusing on a recent algorithmic improvement to the Muon optimizer, as proposed in the Polar Express paper (link). It demonstrates a new approach to the gradient-orthogonalization step at the core of the Muon algorithm, claiming the following properties:
1. Better model fit compared to Newton-Schulz (lower validation loss),
2. More stable convergence, and
3. Faster convergence.

Our main avenues of exploration will be the following:

 (A) An empirical study where we sweep hyperparameters for the Polar Express implementation. Our goal is to find optimal hyperparameter values and characterize how big of an effect they have on convergence behavior and model fit. This will produce interesting results in all cases: either we find a better set of parameters than published in the paper , or we show that this algorithm is robust or sensitive to variations in the hyperparameter. 

(B) For a more ambitious sub-project (time-permitting), we will attempt to show that attention layers can be trained more stably with Muon + Polar Express compared to the traditional Muon + Newton-Schulz.

For (A), each datapoint in our sweep will be the result of training the small and medium GPT-2 language models on a few 10's of millions of tokens of the FineWeb dataset. All hyperparameters for this training will be identical to those quoted in the paper to isolate the effect of different implementations of the polar decomposition subroutine of the Muon optimizer. 

For (B), we are less certain about the specifics at this time and are in the process of reviewing the literature.

Note: Our group will likely have access to sufficient external compute for at least part (A).
